messages.subject: Rotation and h2 vector
messages.body_plain:
Phil,

I noticed that, when loadings of multidimensional IRT models are rotated, the h2 column stays the same.  Unless I don't understand h2 (I think it is just the sum of squared loadings in each row), it seems that h2 should change when rotation is performed.  I have some example code below that illustrates the issue.

Thanks,
Ed

library(mirt)
data(SAT12)
data <- SAT12[,1:6]

## Fit 2-factor model and obtain rotated loadings
(m1 <- mirt(data, 2, 'graded'))
rot.loadings <- summary(m1)

## Seems like h2 should be based on the rotated loading matrix:
rot.h2 <- rowSums(rot.loadings$rotF^2)

## Instead, the "unrotated" h2 (from the original model object)
## appears to display with rotated loadings
h2 <- rowSums(m1@F^2)
all.equal(h2, as.numeric(rot.loadings$h2))

messages.subject: Re: Rotation and h2 vector
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ed,

That's correct, the h2 stat is in most cases (i.e., 2PL and graded
models) equivalent to the communality estimate in EFA, and has the
same interpretation as well. It is invariant to rotation, which is why
it remains unchanged. However, the property that h2 = Σ Fi2 only holds
when the axes are in an orthogonal orientation (e.g., using
summary(mod, rotate = 'none'), or summary(mod, rotate = 'varimax')),
otherwise you have to do a bit more work to obtain it. Hope that
helps.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Guess and Upper don´t be fixed
messages.subject_clean: Guess and Upper don´t be fixed
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeremias,

I think I understand what you are asking, but please correct me if I'm off. To estimate the lower and upper bound parameters you need to change the default itemtype= ... argument. To estimate only the lower bound, you can choose the '3PL' model, and to estimate both upper and lower use itemtype='4PL' (or give a character vector specifying mixed item types).

Changing the guess= and upper= inputs will change the starting values of these inputs, but not freely estimate them. This is mainly because these parameters are extremely difficult to estimate, and often require informative priors (i.e., 'logit' priors, see the examples in ?mirt using the LSAT7 dataset). Hope that helps.

Phil
